title: Work
deck: Asking good questions, building the right tools, and doing the work that connects them.
opening: An AI can research a subject, write software, or build an interactive explanation. What should you ask it to do? Much of the work is inside that question: understanding the problem, finding missing information, defining success, and noticing when an impressive answer solves the wrong thing.

For roughly three years, I have been immersed in large language models: following their intellectual and practical frontier and experimenting with how to think and make things with them. I approach this as a generalist, interested in underlying questions as well as tools. Earlier research roles at Kantar TNS and GfK International taught me to carry a question through investigation, fieldwork and analysis to findings I could explain.

Capable agents expand the technical and subject territory I can explore. I contribute inquiry, requirements, direction and judgment; agents contribute substantial research, implementation, drafting and testing. Together we can learn unfamiliar territory, develop tools and workflows, and test an idea against the work it should serve.
aspiration: I want what we can attempt to become things people can use, understand or enjoy. The missing piece might be software, a better question, or an experiment small enough to reveal what the grand proposal missed. I am interested in finding that piece and making it.

cases.title: Research: ask both sides of the same question
body: Were health and social policies reaching older people? At Kantar TNS / BRIMA, I led a study combining interviews with policy stakeholders and a nationally representative survey of older people. Knowing what a policy intended and knowing how people experienced it required different sources.

I carried the work through design, field coordination, analysis, reporting and presentation. My wider history includes telecom user experience, projects for UNICEF and UNDP, and USAID-funded civil-society research at Kantar.

cases.title: Knowledge compiler: the number changed; did the advice?
body: A method takes four minutes rather than eight. Then a correction adds six minutes of setup. In the fictional Lumen example, the question is whether the recommendation changes with the arithmetic.

I directed an AI-assisted knowledge compiler separating source snapshots, claims and interpretation, building on Karpathy’s LLM Wiki idea and earlier Claude work. The walkthrough preserves the old reasoning while revising the time-saving conclusion. Structural checks keep the record intact; deciding what follows still takes judgment.

cases.title: Harness Engine: what does “track deliveries” mean?
body: Which date counts? Which document takes priority? What happens when quantities disagree? These are requirements hiding inside a two-word task. Harness Engine uses interviews anchored in working documents to recover them, keeping the knowledge separate from the AI instructions generated from it.

I directed successive AI-assisted iterations. The repository includes correction routes and a runnable package-check demonstration; the complete flow still needs validation in a user’s installed environment.
cases.label: Inspect the project and demonstration

cases.title: Air pollution: an obvious problem, a difficult solution
body: Everyone benefits from cleaner air. But a policy still meets households with limited means, firms with their own incentives, and a government facing difficult choices. My 2018 essay connects the public-health problem with these economic and political constraints, examining what proposed remedies would ask of people.

I wrote the English original, “Air pollution in Macedonia: facing the inevitable tragedy of the commons.” An adapted Macedonian version was published under my byline by Deutsche Welle on 13 January 2018. It is a historical writing sample.
cases.label: Read the published Macedonian essay

supporting: Cyborgism / Personal AI OS explores what the next session needs beyond a transcript: decisions, reasons and unresolved disagreements. I also plan a collection and benchmark drawn from my own AI interactions and questions, to study the situations where I actually need help. That collection remains to be built.
creative: I publish essays and selected AI-assisted visual work, and want to make ideas approachable through demonstrations, learning experiences and forms worth playing with. Some work should be useful; some can invite us to notice, imagine or enjoy something.
invitation: If you have a difficult question, a process that needs a better tool, or knowledge you want other people to understand, I would like to hear about it. I am open to employment, independent projects and creative collaboration.

For a team exploring AI, I can investigate the work, learn unfamiliar territory, define requirements, direct agents in making a concrete attempt, and test and refine it with its users. An investigation might reveal a useful workflow, a teaching need, or a reason to change the proposal before building more.
Bring the question, the documents, the awkward example or the unfinished attempt. Tell me what you hope could become possible and who it would matter to. We can begin there.
short_bio: Petre Laskov combines research, practical AI, writing and learning. He directs capable agents toward useful tools, workflows and explanations. His earlier research roles were at Kantar TNS and GfK International.
